questions.text: What distinguishes MuZero from AlphaZero in the lesson’s comparison?

options.A: MuZero trains a value network but never searches; AlphaZero searches with MCTS.
options.B: MuZero learns latent dynamics for search; AlphaZero searches using known game rules.
options.C: MuZero uses group-relative rewards; AlphaZero uses a learned reward model.
options.D: MuZero requires human move labels; AlphaZero trains only from game outcomes.

questions.explanation: AlphaZero searches using known game rules, while MuZero learns a latent dynamics and reward model and runs search in that learned space.

questions.text: You want to train a reasoning policy with GRPO on coding tasks. What must supply a dependable reward for sampled solutions?

options.A: A diverse set of past opponent policies for league play.
options.B: A learned simulator of latent code execution dynamics.
options.C: A trusted verifier that tests whether each solution is correct.
options.D: A value critic that predicts every token’s expected return.

questions.explanation: The lesson’s GRPO setup scores sampled completions with a verifier, such as tests for code or an exact answer checker, then forms group-relative advantages.

questions.text: In the lesson’s grpo_step, one group has rewards [1, 1, 1, 1]. The code computes each advantage as (r − mean_r)/(std_r + 1e−8). What is every advantage?

options.A: 1, because every sampled answer passed the verifier.
options.B: 0, because each reward equals the group mean.
options.C: 0.25, because each reward is one quarter of the total.
options.D: Undefined, because the code divides by an exact zero.

questions.explanation: The group mean is 1, so each numerator r−mean is 0. The small denominator offset prevents division by zero; every advantage is 0.
